title: Session border controllers
summary: Deployment requirements, the B2BUA role, and the functions whose limits stay on the vendor datasheet.

lessons.title: RFC 5853 is requirements, not a protocol
lessons.summary: RFC 5853 collects requirements from SBC deployments. It does not define an SBC wire protocol.
objectives: Classify RFC 5853 as informational
Name functions operators ask an SBC to perform
Keep those functions separate from SIP methods

illustration.title: Requirements sit above SIP
illustration.caption: RFC 5853 describes deployments. SIP, SDP, and RTP keep their own specifications.

layers.name: SDP and RTP
layers.detail: Offer, answer, and the media packets

paragraphs: There is no single protocol RFC that defines an SBC. RFC 5853 is informational requirements gathered from SBC deployments.
The document does not add a SIP method, a response code, or a header that every SBC must speak. INVITE, OPTIONS, and 200 OK remain the RFC 3261 messages you already read.

Topology hiding, media anchoring, media bypass, transcoding, DTMF interworking, OPTIONS keepalives, and call admission show up as deployment functions. Each one is implemented by a product, on top of SIP and RTP.
Session limits and calls-per-second figures are platform-specific and must come from the vendor datasheet. This track does not invent a counter name or a formula for them.

quiz.q: RFC 5853 is
choices: The protocol specification of an SBC
quiz.why: It records what deployments asked SBCs to do. It does not define a new wire protocol.

quiz.q: Which statement matches the status of an SBC specification?
choices: No single protocol RFC defines an SBC
RFC 3261 section 4 is the SBC protocol
RFC 7092 is a media codec list
ITU-T G.711 is the SBC signaling RFC
quiz.why: RFC 7092 taxonomizes B2BUAs. G.711 is a codec recommendation.

quiz.q: Call-capacity numbers for an SBC belong in
choices: The vendor datasheet for that platform
RFC 5853 as a universal CPS formula
quiz.why: Limits are platform-specific. Do not invent a calls-per-second formula.

quiz.q: Topology hiding is best classified as
quiz.why: RFC 5853 treats it as a requirement seen in deployments.

quiz.q: An OPTIONS keepalive uses
quiz.why: OPTIONS is the standard capability request. The interval is product configuration.

quiz.q: Media transcoding capacity should be taken from
quiz.why: RFC 3264 defines offer/answer, not a session budget.

cards.back: Informational requirements from SBC deployments. Not an SBC protocol.
INVITE and OPTIONS stay as RFC 3261 defined them.
Session and transcode limits are platform-specific.
The usual SIP role behind an SBC. Taxonomy is RFC 7092.

lessons.title: An SBC is commonly a B2BUA
lessons.summary: RFC 7092 taxonomizes B2BUAs. An SBC is commonly a UAS on one side and a UAC on the other, not a pure proxy.
objectives: Contrast a B2BUA with a pure proxy
Point at two dialogs in one call
Use RFC 7092 as the taxonomy

illustration.title: Two dialogs, one call
illustration.caption: The inbound side is a UAS dialog. The outbound side is a new UAC dialog.

sections.h: UAS on one side, UAC on the other
paragraphs: A back-to-back user agent receives a request and processes it as a UAS. To continue the call it acts as a UAC and generates a new request.
RFC 3261 defines that concatenation. RFC 7092 taxonomizes the B2BUAs that products actually build, including SBCs that also touch media.
A pure proxy forwards the same request and adds its own Via. It does not create a second dialog with a new Call-ID just to hide the first hop.
An SBC is commonly a B2BUA. The outbound INVITE in this synthetic uses Call-ID b2bua-legb-01@example.com while the caller still uses Call-ID a84b4c76e66710@example.com.

quiz.q: RFC 7092 is
quiz.why: It classifies B2BUAs. It is not a second SIP.

quiz.q: On the caller side an SBC commonly behaves as a
quiz.why: It must produce responses for the dialog it accepted.

quiz.q: On the callee side an SBC commonly behaves as a
choices: UAC that generates a new request
quiz.why: The outbound request is a new client transaction.

quiz.q: A pure proxy typically
choices: Forwards the request and adds Via
Mints a new Call-ID and drops the caller Via stack
quiz.why: Via accumulation is proxy behavior. A B2BUA builds a new request.

quiz.q: In the synthetic ladder the outbound Call-ID is
choices: The same value as Alice’s Call-ID
quiz.why: The new Call-ID is the visible sign of the second dialog.

quiz.q: Dialog state on a B2BUA is
choices: Maintained on each leg it creates
quiz.why: RFC 3261 says a B2BUA maintains dialog state and participates in requests on those dialogs.

cards.back: UAS plus UAC. Two dialogs for one call.
Forwards the request and adds Via.
Often different on the two legs of an SBC.
Defines the B2BUA as UAS concatenated with UAC.

lessons.title: Topology hiding rewrites the addresses you leak
lessons.summary: Topology hiding replaces caller addresses in signaling and, when media is anchored, in SDP.
objectives: Name the headers that leak topology
See Contact and Via change at the B2BUA
Leave the rewrite policy in the product guide

illustration.title: What this synthetic hides
illustration.caption: Addresses below are the lab’s documentation addresses.

paragraphs: Alice’s INVITE in this lab carries Via 203.0.113.10, Contact sip:alice@203.0.113.10, and an SDP c= line of 203.0.113.10. A Record-Route or User-Agent can leak still more.
A pure proxy would add a Via and forward the rest. Topology hiding is the deployment function that stops those internal names from reaching the carrier.

sections.h: What the carrier is allowed to see
paragraphs: The outbound INVITE uses Via 203.0.113.20, Contact sip:sbc@203.0.113.20, and SDP c=203.0.113.20. The caller Via, the caller Contact, and the User-Agent are not copied.
Which extra headers a product strips is a configuration choice documented by that vendor. RFC 5853 records the requirement. It does not publish one vendor’s header list.

lessons.title: Anchor, bypass, transcode, and DTMF
lessons.summary: Anchoring terminates RTP on the SBC. Bypass lets endpoints exchange media. Transcoding and DTMF interworking need the media path.
objectives: Separate anchoring from bypass
Tie transcoding to an anchored path
Treat DTMF interworking as a media function

paragraphs: Media anchoring means the SBC terminates RTP and originates a second RTP stream. In this lab the inside c= is 203.0.113.10 and the outside c= is 203.0.113.20.
Media bypass leaves a path where the endpoints send RTP to each other. The SBC still handles SIP. The product guide is where bypass conditions are written.
Transcoding converts one codec to another, so the SBC must be on the media path. How many sessions a chassis can transcode is platform-specific and must come from the vendor datasheet.
DTMF interworking converts between RFC 4733 telephone-event and another form the peer understands, such as in-band tones. There is no universal counter for that work in RFC 5853.

lessons.title: OPTIONS keepalives
lessons.summary: SBCs probe a peer with OPTIONS. A 200 OK means the peer answered. The interval is product configuration.
objectives: Build a legal OPTIONS
Read a 200 OK as liveness
Keep the timer out of the RFC

illustration.title: A keepalive, then a call
illustration.caption: RFC 3261 defines OPTIONS. It does not define the SBC’s repeat timer.

paragraphs: OPTIONS queries capabilities. Outside a dialog it is a simple request with its own CSeq method token, which must be OPTIONS.
In this synthetic the SBC at 203.0.113.20 sends OPTIONS to 192.0.2.40. The 200 OK lists Allow and proves the peer produced a response.
Many SBC deployments send OPTIONS on a timer and treat a missing answer as a down peer. That timer is product configuration.
RFC 3261 does not publish an SBC keepalive interval, and this lesson does not invent one. Use the guide for the software you run.

lessons.title: Call admission stays on the datasheet
lessons.summary: An SBC can refuse a new INVITE when its configured budget is exhausted. The number itself is platform-specific.
objectives: Describe admission as a local policy
Read 503 as one documented failure response
Refuse invented capacity formulas

illustration.title: What is specified where
illustration.caption: The SIP code is standard. The session budget is not.
rows: How many sessions this chassis holds

paragraphs: Call admission is a deployment function: the SBC stops accepting new calls when a configured budget is exhausted. The INVITE in this synthetic is refused with 503 Service Unavailable.
RFC 3261 defines 503 as the server being unable to handle the request. Some products choose a different final response. The product guide names the code for that software.
The number of concurrent sessions, the media budget, and any calls-per-second ceiling are platform-specific and must come from the vendor datasheet. RFC 5853 does not publish those numbers.

Do not derive a capacity figure from Max-Forwards, from the UDP port, or from a formula this course does not print. Count the sessions the platform is actually holding and compare that count with the datasheet.

lessons.title: Active and standby, without a made-up timer
lessons.summary: Active/standby is a product behavior. One unit owns the work and the other is ready. Timers belong in that product’s HA guide.
objectives: Describe active/standby at product level
Keep failover timing out of the SIP RFC
Expect dialog state to be a product problem

illustration.title: Roles, not a timer
illustration.caption: How fast the standby reacts is documented by the vendor.

paragraphs: In an active/standby pair, one unit processes signaling and media and the other is ready to take that role. The SIP dialogs in this ladder exist on the active unit at 203.0.113.20.
The standby does not appear as a third SIP hop. Whether established dialogs survive a switch is a product behavior, because a B2BUA holds dialog state that a bare packet forward would not.

sections.h: No failover timer in this course
paragraphs: Detection methods and failover timing differ by product. This lesson does not invent a failover timer, a hello interval, or a session-recovery count.
When a design needs a number, take it from the HA chapter for the software version you run. Do not copy a timer from a different chassis and do not look for it in RFC 5853.

quiz.q: Active/standby describes
choices: A product pair where one unit owns the work
quiz.why: It is high-availability behavior, not a protocol role in RFC 3261.

quiz.q: The standby in this ladder
choices: Does not appear as a SIP hop
Inserts a second Via on every request
quiz.why: SIP shows the active dialogs only.

quiz.q: A failover timer should come from
choices: The HA guide for that software
quiz.why: This course intentionally states no timer.

quiz.q: Dialog survival across a switch is
choices: A product behavior, because a B2BUA holds dialog state
Guaranteed by RFC 3261 for every proxy
quiz.why: The taxonomy explains why state exists. The product explains whether it moves.

quiz.q: Inventing a three-second failover value would be
choices: Outside both the RFC and this course
quiz.why: Timers stay in the product HA chapter.

quiz.q: The active signaling address in the shared ladder is
quiz.why: That is the SBC address in the lab topology.

cards.back: The unit currently processing the dialogs.
Ready to take the role. Not a SIP method.
Do not invent a failover interval.
A B2BUA holds it. Survival is a product question.

lab.title: Count the SIP hops
lab.prompt: Play the call. How many SIP roles does the standby occupy in the ladder?
steps: Notice the standby is not among them.

check.q: The standby appears in the SIP ladder as
check.why: HA state is outside the message flow until the product switches.

fault.title: A timer copied from another product
fault.symptom: After the active unit stops responding, the standby does not own 203.0.113.20. The design used a failover timer taken from a different vendor’s blog.
fault.log:
INVITE sip:+15551212@203.0.113.20 SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bK7766as01
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
(no response from 203.0.113.20)
choices: Failover timing is product-specific and was not taken from this product’s HA guide
RFC 5853 sets failover to one SDP ptime
The Call-ID must change before the standby answers
fault.why: The capture shows silence from the active address. It does not contain a universal timer.
fault.cause: The pair was operated with a failover value that this product’s guide does not use.
fault.fix: Open the HA chapter for the software you run and configure detection as that chapter describes. Do not import a timer from a different platform.
